paragraphs.title: Introduction, Crisis, and a Plea for Healing

easy.explanation: The psalm is introduced as a miktam of David.
easy.q: To whom is this psalm attributed in its introduction?

easy.explanation: The KJV says, “Thou hast made the earth to tremble.”
easy.q: What did God make the earth do?

easy.explanation: The speaker asks God to “heal the breaches thereof.”
easy.q: What does the speaker ask God to heal?

medium.explanation: The passage speaks of being cast off, a broken earth, and hard things.
medium.q: Which sequence best describes the condition of the people in this passage?

medium.explanation: The phrase describes the troubling experience God has made the people endure.
medium.q: What does “the wine of astonishment” represent in context?

answers: The brokenness leads to a plea for God to heal it
The brokenness proves that the people have already won
The brokenness leads to a request to divide the land
medium.explanation: After saying that the earth is broken, the speaker asks God to heal its breaches.
medium.q: How are the broken earth and the request for healing related?

answers: The crisis is connected with severe national trouble
The difficult circumstances have no connection to the psalm
challenge.explanation: The passage presents the people’s suffering against a background of serious conflict and distress.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the connection between the difficult circumstances and the people’s condition?

answers: A sense of abandonment and a request for restoration
A declaration about dividing the land
challenge.explanation: The words express the people’s feeling of abandonment and their desire for God to turn to them again.
challenge.q: What does the appeal, “O God, thou hast cast us off,” express?

answers: A description of enemies being humbled
A national crisis followed by a plea for healing
challenge.explanation: The verses describe rejection, shaking, hard circumstances, and a request for restoration.
challenge.q: Which idea unites the verses in this section?

paragraphs.title: Banner, Rescue, and the Promise of Victory

easy.explanation: The KJV says, “Thou hast given a banner to them that fear thee.”
easy.q: To whom did God give a banner?

easy.explanation: The verse says that the banner was to be displayed “because of the truth.”
easy.q: Why was the banner to be displayed?

easy.explanation: The speaker asks, “That thy beloved may be delivered.”
easy.q: What does the speaker ask God to do for his beloved?

answers: To express hope and divine faithfulness
medium.explanation: The banner is a public sign connected with truth, courage, and God’s favor.
medium.q: What is the purpose of the banner in this passage?

medium.explanation: A banner is a visible sign or flag displayed before the people.
medium.q: In this context, what is a “banner”?

answers: The banner removes every need for help
The banner encourages hope while deliverance is still requested
The banner describes only the enemies
medium.explanation: Although the banner is a sign of hope, the people still ask God to save them.
medium.q: How are the banner and the request for deliverance connected?

challenge.explanation: In the context of the psalm, “thy beloved” refers to God’s people who need deliverance.
challenge.q: Who are most likely meant by “thy beloved” in this passage?

answers: The psalm moves from distress toward a sign of hope and rescue
The psalm moves from dividing the land to describing a city wall
The psalm moves from victory to complete abandonment
challenge.explanation: The banner introduces hope, while the prayer asks for God’s saving response.
challenge.q: What change in thought occurs from the crisis in the previous section to this passage?

answers: The people seek protection and hope under God’s sign
The people intend to abandon the conflict
challenge.explanation: The banner represents encouragement and faith, while the prayer seeks God’s protection and rescue.
challenge.q: What does the combination of displaying the banner and asking God to save suggest?

paragraphs.title: Israel’s Unity and the Distribution of the Land

answers: Divide Shechem and measure the valley
easy.explanation: The KJV says, “I will divide Shechem, and mete out the valley of Succoth.”
easy.q: What does the speaker say he will do with Shechem and the valley of Succoth?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “Ephraim also is the strength of mine head.”
easy.q: Which tribe is called “the strength of mine head”?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “Judah is my lawgiver.”

answers: The division and ordering of the land
medium.explanation: God’s declaration is followed by the speaker’s intention to divide Shechem and measure Succoth.
medium.q: What does God announce in this passage?

medium.explanation: To mete out means to measure or assign portions.
medium.q: What does “mete out” mean in “mete out the valley of Succoth”?

answers: They represent the enemies of Israel
They represent the tribes united under Israel’s rule
medium.explanation: The tribal names present Israel as an ordered and united people.
medium.q: How do the names of Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Judah function in the passage?

answers: They are portrayed as enemies of one another
They are viewed as parts of a unified Israel
They have no connection with the subject of the psalm
challenge.explanation: The tribes are listed together as parts of one national and political order.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from placing several tribes together in this passage?

answers: The declaration makes victory and orderly possession imaginable
The declaration makes the land unimportant
The declaration describes only the enemy’s condition
challenge.explanation: God’s spoken promise gives confidence that the land can be possessed and arranged.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between God’s declaration and the measuring of the land?

answers: Leadership and authority among the united people
challenge.explanation: The phrase presents Judah as associated with rule, law, and national leadership.
challenge.q: What governing idea appears in the phrase “Judah is my lawgiver”?

paragraphs.title: Dominance over the Enemy and Trust in God’s Help

easy.explanation: The passage names Moab, Edom, and Philistia.
easy.q: Which enemies are named in this section?

answers: Into the strong city and to Edom
easy.explanation: The speaker asks, “Who will bring me into the strong city? who will lead me into Edom?”
easy.q: Where does the speaker ask to be led?

easy.explanation: The conclusion says, “Through God we shall do valiantly.”
easy.q: Through whom will the people do valiantly?

answers: Human help by itself is insufficient
The enemy is the source of salvation
medium.explanation: The statement contrasts unreliable human help with dependence upon God.
medium.q: What does “vain is the help of man” teach?

medium.explanation: The enemies are the opposing nations described in the passage.
medium.q: What does “our enemies” mean in the concluding phrase?

answers: The enemies will be humbled, but guidance to the strong city is still needed
The enemies will win, so guidance is unnecessary
medium.explanation: The speaker trusts that God will tread down the enemies while still asking God to lead the people.
medium.q: How does the passage combine confidence about the enemies with a request for guidance?

answers: The division of the land and the names of the tribes
The weakness of human help and the power of God’s help
The banner and the healing of the earth
challenge.explanation: The conclusion contrasts “vain is the help of man” with victory through God.
challenge.q: What is the central contrast at the end of the psalm?

answers: He depends on God throughout the journey, not only at its end
He is giving up the struggle
He prefers human help to God’s help
challenge.explanation: The speaker seeks God’s direction toward the strong city and trusts God for the victory.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the speaker asking both for guidance and for victory?

answers: The enemies are too strong and there is no hope
Victory depends only on dividing the land
God enables his people to overcome their enemies
challenge.explanation: The final verse states that through God the people will act valiantly and God will tread down their enemies.
challenge.q: Which idea best summarizes the final section?
